body:
Kind: Epic · Place: the whole product

## Why

Overworld should be built the way it asks others to build: from clearly expressed behaviours, with a constant dialogue between people and agents, and with progress you can see on the map. See [VISION.md](https://github.com/keneasson/overworld/blob/main/VISION.md).

Today an agent learns what to build from a chat that scrolls away. This epic makes Overworld's own issues the source of truth. People and agents shape an area together, decisions stay pinned to the place they concern, and GitHub Issues is the durable store underneath.

## Behaviours

- BUILD-01 Given an issue marked Ready in Overworld, when an agent asks what to work on, then it gets that issue with everything it needs, without reading a chat history.
- BUILD-02 Given a pull request that closes an issue, when it opens and when it merges, then the issue's place on the map shows in progress and then done, with no one editing it by hand.
- BUILD-03 Given a decision that affects several issues in one area, when the team agrees it in Overworld, then all of those issues change together and reach GitHub, guaranteed, eventually.
- BUILD-04 Given a question raised during work, when it is recorded, then it appears as Fog on the right part of the map until someone answers it.

## Acceptance

- Overworld's own roadmap is mapped from this repository and kept current by the lifecycle.
- At least one child issue is implemented by an agent working from Overworld rather than from a chat prompt.

## Out of scope

- Jira integration (a later stretch goal).
- Accounts and billing (a separate epic).

## Open questions

None at the epic level. Each child carries its own.
title: Epic: Overworld builds itself

body:
Part of #1
Kind: Feature · Place: api/engine (mapping) and the map's layers

## Why

The lifecycle is the contract between people and agents: what can be worked on, what is under way, what is waiting on a decision. Before anything can enforce it, the map has to read it and show it, deterministically, from what is already on GitHub.

## Behaviours

- LIFE-01 Given an open issue labelled `status:draft`, `status:needs-decision`, `status:ready` or `status:in-progress`, when the repository is mapped, then the item shows that state.
- LIFE-02 Given an issue closed as *completed*, when mapped, then it shows Done; given one closed as *not planned*, then it shows Rejected and is drawn as a ruin (faded) rather than removed.
- LIFE-03 Given an open pull request that says `Closes #N`, when mapped, then issue N shows In progress even if its label hasn't caught up.
- LIFE-04 Given an issue whose `## Open questions` section has content, when mapped, then it shows Needs decision and sits in the Fog, whatever its label says.
- LIFE-05 Given an issue with no status label or more than one, when mapped, then it is flagged "status unclear" and the 📍 note says why.
- LIFE-06 Given the map, when the Lifecycle layer is chosen, then each state has its own colour and legend entry, and its counts roll up through every zoom level.

## Acceptance

- Behaviours LIFE-01 to LIFE-06 are covered by tests in `api/test/engine.test.mjs` and `web/test`.
- Mapping `keneasson/overworld` shows this epic and its children in their real states.
- Repositories without status labels map exactly as before.

## Out of scope

- Writing labels back to GitHub, and webhooks (those need the GitHub App; see the sync issue).
- Editing an issue's state from Overworld.

## Open questions
title: Lifecycle: read each issue's state from GitHub and show it on the map

body:
Part of #1
Kind: Feature · Place: api/model and a sync worker

## Why

Teams decide things about an *area*, and one decision changes many issues. GitHub edits one issue at a time and can be slow or rate-limited. Overworld needs changesets: groups of edits that are discussed, accepted together, and then reach GitHub, guaranteed but eventually.

## Behaviours

- SYNC-01 Given edits to several issues in one area, when they're grouped as a changeset, then they can be reviewed, commented on and accepted or discarded as one.
- SYNC-02 Given an accepted changeset, when GitHub is slow, rate-limited or down, then every edit still arrives in order, with retries, and nothing is lost or applied twice.
- SYNC-03 Given an edit made directly on GitHub, when the webhook arrives, then Overworld updates; if it conflicts with a pending changeset, the conflicting sections are shown to a person rather than overwritten.
- SYNC-04 Given any drift (a missed webhook, say), when the nightly reconciliation runs, then Overworld and GitHub agree again and the run reports what it fixed.
- SYNC-05 Given the lifecycle rules, when labels drift on GitHub (two status labels, say), then Overworld repairs them.

## Acceptance

- A transactional outbox in the single table, a worker with a dead-letter queue, and access patterns documented in `api/model/README.md`.
- A test that kills the worker mid-sync and shows the sync completes after restart.

## Out of scope

- Real-time co-editing (its own issue).

## Open questions

- Set up a GitHub App (its permissions, webhook URL, and where its private key lives in `.conf/` and in AWS)? It's needed for writing to issues and receiving webhooks. Proposed: yes, created under keneasson.
- Conflict policy: merge section by section and ask only on a real clash? Or always ask?
title: Changesets and guaranteed sync to GitHub Issues

body:
Part of #1
Kind: Feature · Place: a new MCP endpoint beside the API

## Why

Agents shouldn't scrape web pages or read whole chat histories. An MCP server lets Claude Code, or any other agent, use the map the way people do: zoom to an area, find ready work, get the whole context of one issue, claim it, and raise questions that stay on the map.

## Behaviours

- MCP-01 `zoom(place)` returns that area and its children, each with title, summary, state and counts. This is the same semantic zoom people get.
- MCP-02 `next_ready()` returns ready, unclaimed work, ordered by priority and dependency.
- MCP-03 `context(issue)` returns the parent chain, siblings, behaviours, decisions, open questions, the files it lives in, and linked pull requests, in a form an agent reads in one pass.
- MCP-04 `claim(issue)` gives a time-limited claim; a second claimant is refused and told who holds it.
- MCP-05 `ask(issue, question)` adds an open question, moves the issue to Needs decision and puts it in the Fog.
- MCP-06 `propose(changeset)` submits edits for people to review; an agent never rewrites an issue silently.

## Acceptance

- Works from Claude Code with a single `claude mcp add` command.
- Every tool's response is deterministic and covered by tests.

## Out of scope

- AI reading of issues (the metered tier).

## Open questions

- How do agents authenticate: a per-user token made in Overworld, or OAuth? Proposed: a token now, OAuth when accounts exist.
- Should it run inside the existing Lambda (streamable HTTP) or as a separate function?
title: MCP server: agents use the map the way people do

body:
Part of #1
Kind: Feature · Place: the web app's item panel and editor

## Why

Writing a good issue should be easier in Overworld than on GitHub. The editor works on the strict shape (Why, Behaviours, Acceptance, Out of scope, Open questions) and lets a team edit across an area, not one issue at a time.

## Behaviours

- EDIT-01 Given an item, when it is opened for editing, then each section is its own rich-text field, and the markdown saved to GitHub is exactly the strict shape.
- EDIT-02 Given behaviours, when they are added, then each gets the next ID for its area and can be written as Given / When / Then.
- EDIT-03 Given an area, when someone opens it, then they can edit several of its items side by side and the edits collect into one changeset.
- EDIT-04 Given a comment on a single behaviour or section, when the item is viewed, then the comment is anchored there and travels with it.
- EDIT-05 Given a phone, when editing, then the same editor works in the mobile browser.

## Acceptance

- Round-trip test: GitHub markdown → editor → markdown is unchanged for well-formed issues.

## Out of scope

- Live cursors and simultaneous typing (the next issue).

## Open questions

- TipTap (ProseMirror) is the proposed editor. Any objection, or a preference for Lexical or BlockNote?
title: Area editor for the strict issue shape

body:
Part of #1
Kind: Feature · Place: a real-time sync service

## Why

Reviewing an area together means seeing each other: who is here, where their cursor is, and what they're typing. That needs a server that holds open connections, which Lambda can't do.

## Behaviours

- LIVE-01 Given two or more people in the same area, when one types, then the others see it within a second, and simultaneous edits merge without loss (Yjs CRDT).
- LIVE-02 Given people and agents in an area, when it is viewed, then each one's presence and cursor shows on the map.
- LIVE-03 Given a dropped connection, when it returns, then offline edits merge cleanly.
- LIVE-04 Given no one in an area, when it's idle, then the service costs nothing.

## Acceptance

- Two browsers and one agent editing the same area at once, with no lost edits.

## Out of scope

- The Kanban-style board view.

## Open questions

- Where should it run? Cloudflare Durable Objects running Yjs (y-partyserver) is proposed: billed per use, scales to zero, with a free tier. The alternative is Hocuspocus on Fargate, which keeps everything on AWS but costs about $15 a month or more even when idle.
title: Live co-editing of an area
